summary:
Van is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework: the Turkish penal code, migration rules, health regulations and prison administration apply here in full. No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for Van itself, and that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence rather than local permissiveness.

A leaked omnibus measure identified by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 as the "11th Judicial Package" would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility assessment and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns that its passage would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey has become explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice, according to Kaos GL's 2025 review "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People". Public institutions received "Year of the Family" instructions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The same monitoring records 313 liberty violations in 2025, about two and a half times the previous year, with 299 detention decisions; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, among them obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; and 61 travel bans.

These national patterns reach a visitor directly at document checkpoints. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance, so any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation. Street-level enforcement is documented in Istanbul, where in 2025 police held roughly 20 trans women for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Comparable policing practice in Van is not separately documented.

Trans prisoners in Turkey are placed according to registered sex. Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, a trans man had been held in a women's prison, and the case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation, including arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and an administration operating on a binary basis with no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the "other" option in gender reassignment reports and required electronic reporting, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. All of these rules operate in Van.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement of the pending draft legislation has in places preceded its passage. Reporting from Istanbul in 2025 records trans women stopped and documented under police background checks while stating that no law had yet been passed, indicating that hostility already operates through discretionary policing rather than statutory authority alone.

Street-level enforcement is documented most heavily in Istanbul, the largest city, and the absence of equivalent reporting for Van reflects documentation concentration rather than evidence of lighter practice in the province.

The pattern of state asymmetry in response to violence predates the current policy turn. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, an outcome activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
localsOnly:
Residents of Van live under the same "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions that Kaos GL identifies as the administrative expression of the 2025 policy turn, and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation signals the operating space available to local advocacy groups.

Private-life violations recorded nationally rose from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, so continuity of hormone access is a documented resident concern rather than a visitor issue.

The 61 travel bans recorded in 2025 constrain residents' movement across the country, and the placement of trans prisoners by registered sex governs the sentence served by any resident convicted of an offence.

The September 2025 Health Ministry regulation requiring electronic gender reassignment reports and barring the "other" option shapes how residents' identity documents and medical records are generated, with implications for anyone seeking to change registered markers.

Residents face the same custody conditions documented for LGBT detainees generally: arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints procedures described as ineffective and capable of attracting further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the "11th Judicial Package" reported on 29 October 2025 has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not resolved in the sources available for this record; it is reported here as a leaked draft in pending status.

No enforcement data, arrest records, incident reports or policing directives specific to Van were located in the source inventory. The province-level entry therefore carries the national framework and an explicit note of absent documentation, which should not be read as evidence that practice in Van differs from Istanbul or other provinces.

The current reach of the 2008 Human Rights Watch findings is unresolved: that report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is included as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of present law.

Van-specific information on Pride events, LGBT venues, local health provision for transition care and the operation of provincial police checkpoints is not sourced and remains unverified.

It is not established from these sources whether the private-life violations involving obstruction of hormone therapy occurred in state or private health facilities, nor whether any such obstruction has been recorded in Van.
